overview.text: A capacitor is an electrical component that stores separated charge: its conducting parts hold equal amounts of positive and negative charge, usually with an insulating material between them. This arrangement creates an electric field, and the capacitor’s energy is stored in that field. Capacitance describes how much charge is stored for a given voltage, so it is calculated as charge divided by voltage. Its SI unit is the farad, equal to one coulomb per volt. Capacitors are useful in circuits for tasks such as filtering static from radio reception and storing energy for heart defibrillators.

key_facts.text: A typical capacitor has two nearby conductors that do not touch; an insulator, called a dielectric, often separates them.
Charging a capacitor separates equal positive and negative charges onto its conductors, while the capacitor as a whole remains neutral.
Capacitance is charge divided by voltage: C = Q/V. A larger capacitance means more charge stored for the same voltage.
The farad (F) is the SI unit of capacitance; one farad equals one coulomb per volt.
A charged capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its conductors; its energy can be calculated as U = ½CV².
